section.title: Rejection and the Death of John
section.sectionRationale: After the parables, the shadow of rejection deepens. Jesus is dishonored in His own hometown, where familiarity breeds unbelief, and Matthew then recounts the brutal execution of John the Baptist by a weak, guilt-ridden Herod. The forerunner's fate at the hands of a cowardly king foreshadows the path of rejection and death that awaits Jesus Himself.
section.thesis: The One rejected in His hometown by unbelief and the forerunner beheaded by a cowardly king together reveal the world's hostility to God's messengers, so that the death of John casts the shadow of the cross over the ministry of Jesus, the prophet without honor.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Jesus dishonored and hindered by unbelief in Nazareth; Herod's guilty fear that Jesus is John raised; and the account of John's imprisonment and beheading.

verses.text: Coming to His {{patris|hometown}}, He taught the people in their synagogue, and they were astonished. “Where did this man get such wisdom and miraculous powers?” they asked.
“Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t His mother’s name Mary, and aren’t His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas?
Aren’t all His sisters with us as well? Where then did this man get all these things?”
And they {{skandalizo|took offense}} at Him. But Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown and in his own household is a {{prophetes|prophet}} without honor.”
And He did not do many miracles there, because of their {{apistia|unbelief}}.

units.label: Herod's guilty fear
units.note: this is John, risen from the dead

verses.text: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the reports about Jesus
and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him.”
Now Herod had arrested John and bound him and put him in prison on account of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife,
because John had been telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.”
Although Herod wanted to kill John, he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet.
On Herod’s birthday, however, the daughter of Herodias danced before them and pleased Herod
so much that he promised with an oath to give to her whatever she asked.
Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”
The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered that her wish be granted
and sent to have John beheaded in the prison.
John’s head was brought in on a platter and presented to the girl, who carried it to her mother.
Then John’s disciples came and took his body and buried it. And they went and informed Jesus.

patris.gloss: Hometown, native place. Jesus returns to Nazareth, where He grew up, and finds not faith but offense; those who knew Him as the carpenter's son cannot see past the familiar to the glory before them.

skandalizo.gloss: To stumble, take offense, be tripped up. The townspeople are scandalized by Jesus, tripping over His ordinary origins; the same word describes those who fall away, for offense at Christ is a barrier to faith.

prophetes.gloss: Prophet, one who speaks for God. Jesus applies the proverb that a prophet is without honor in his hometown to Himself, placing His rejection in the long line of God's spokesmen dishonored by their own people.

apistia.gloss: Unbelief, lack of faith. It is because of their unbelief that Jesus did not do many miracles in Nazareth; not that His power failed, but that His mighty works met faith, not spectacle for hardened hearts.

basic.context: Jesus returns to Nazareth and teaches with astonishing wisdom, but the people cannot get past knowing His family: is this not the carpenter's son? They take offense, and He does few miracles there because of their unbelief. Matthew then flashes back to how John the Baptist died: imprisoned for rebuking Herod's unlawful marriage, John is beheaded when Herod, trapped by a rash oath at a birthday feast, grants the request of Herodias's dancing daughter.
basic.hermeneutics: Read these two rejections together. The hometown unbelief shows how familiarity can blind people to Christ. The death of John is told as a grim foreshadowing: a faithful prophet killed by a weak ruler to save face echoes what will happen to Jesus. Matthew places John's martyrdom here, out of strict sequence, to deepen the theme of rejection.
basic.originalLanguages: In His hometown Jesus meets not faith but offense; the people stumble over His ordinary origins. He calls Himself a prophet without honor among his own. And He does few miracles there because of their unbelief, not a failure of power but the absence of the faith to which His works answered.
basic.typology: Jesus stands in the line of rejected prophets, dishonored by His own as they were. John dies as Elijah-like prophets often suffered, opposed by a wicked queen, recalling Elijah and Jezebel. And John's martyrdom foreshadows the greater rejection and death of the One he prepared the way for.
basic.christ: Jesus is the prophet without honor, rejected by those who knew Him best, whose true glory is hidden from unbelief. And He is the One whose forerunner's death prefigures His own: John, faithful to the end, is killed by a cowardly king, just as Jesus will be handed over by weak rulers to keep the crowd content.
basic.god: God's messengers are often dishonored and killed, yet God's purposes advance through their faithfulness and even their deaths. He is not thwarted by unbelief or by wicked kings; the rejection of His prophets and His Son is folded into His saving plan.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 19 shows Elijah persecuted by Jezebel, echoed in John and Herodias. Matthew 17 confirms John as the Elijah who suffered. Jeremiah 11 tells of a prophet rejected in his hometown. And Matthew 27 shows Pilate, like Herod, condemning the innocent to please others.
basic.oneStory: The shadow over Jesus' ministry lengthens. Rejected by His own town and reminded of His forerunner's murder, He walks a path the world has always forced on God's messengers. John dies faithful at the hands of a weak king, and his death points ahead to the cross, where the greater Prophet will be handed over by cowardly rulers, yet through it accomplish salvation.

context.literary:
This section is made of two scenes that seem to have nothing to do with each other, and Matthew has set them side by side on purpose. The first, 13:54 to 58, closes the great parables chapter with a visit that ends in unbelief. The second, 14:1 to 12, opens a new narrative block with a flashback that reaches back in time to explain who Herod is thinking of when he hears of Jesus. Both scenes are about people who cannot see what is in front of them, one because they are too familiar with Jesus and the other because he is too haunted by what he has done.

The Nazareth scene turns on a run of rapid questions, 'Where did this man get...?' repeated in verses 54 and 56, and a list of names that sets Jesus within a family and a trade. The speakers are astonished at His wisdom but reason from His origins. The saying about a prophet's lack of honour, verse 57, is a summary, and the closing verse, 58, is a narrator's verdict with an unusual brevity.

The Herod scene is told as a story within a story. Verses 1 and 2 give the present moment, Herod's guilty speculation, and verses 3 to 12 explain it by going back to John's arrest and death. Jesus does not appear in the account of John's death at all, which is the only extended scene in the Gospel in which He is absent. The narrative is built on contrast. Herod holds a birthday banquet for the great, and it ends in a murder; in the very next scene, Jesus holds a meal in the wilderness for the hungry, and it ends in abundant life, 14:13 to 21. The two tables are meant to be read together.

The structure also builds toward a frame of irony. Herod 'wanted to kill John,' verse 5, but fears the people, and then 'the king was grieved' and kills him anyway, verse 9, because he fears his guests. The man who ruled by fear is ruled by fear.
context.historical:
Nazareth was a small village in lower Galilee, and its synagogue would have been a modest gathering place where the Scriptures were read on the Sabbath and any competent man might be invited to speak. The people knew Jesus' family and trade. 'The carpenter's son' places Him within a working household, and the names James, Joseph, Simon and Judas are what we would expect in a Galilean family of the time. No one expected a prophet to come from so ordinary a background, and the offence was social as much as theological. Luke's account, Luke 4:16 to 30, shows how quickly the reaction turned violent.

Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC until AD 39. He is the Herod of the trial narrative in Luke 23:8 to 11, and Jesus calls him 'that fox,' Luke 13:32. He had married a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas and divorced her to marry Herodias, who had been married to another of his half-brothers and was also his niece. This was a political and a moral scandal. The Law forbade taking a brother's wife, Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21, and John said so publicly, Luke 3:19. The Jewish historian Josephus also reports that Antipas had John put to death, and names the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, as the place of his imprisonment.

The scene of the banquet, as Mark gives it, was a feast for Herod's nobles, military commanders and the leading men of Galilee, Mark 6:21. A dance by a royal daughter before such a gathering, and an oath given before all the guests, put Herod in a position where a refusal would have meant public loss of face. Oaths were taken with great seriousness, and the promise 'up to half my kingdom' in Mark 6:23 echoes the royal formula of Esther 5:3.

John was the most popular prophet of the day, as Matthew 21:26 confirms, and Herod's fear of the crowd was a political reality. His reaction to Jesus in 14:2, that John had been raised, shows how deeply the murder lay on his conscience.
context.canonical:
Jesus' proverb about the prophet without honour is a summary of Israel's history. Moses was challenged in his own camp, Jeremiah was threatened by the men of his own town, Anathoth, Jeremiah 11:21, and told that even his brothers and his father's household had betrayed him, Jeremiah 12:6. The psalmist says, 'I have become a stranger to my brothers,' Psalm 69:8, and the Servant is 'despised and rejected by men,' Isaiah 53:3. John 4:44 records the same saying, and Luke places it at the heart of the Nazareth sermon, adding the examples of Elijah and Elisha, Luke 4:24 to 27. Jesus' own brothers did not believe in Him during His ministry, John 7:5, but after the resurrection James, one of the brothers, becomes a leader of the church, 1 Corinthians 15:7 and Galatians 1:19, and His brothers are praying with the disciples in Acts 1:14.

John's death belongs to the story of Elijah. John dressed like Elijah, 2 Kings 1:8 and Matthew 3:4, and Malachi 4:5 had promised that Elijah would return before the great Day of the LORD. Jesus says plainly that John is 'the Elijah who was to come,' Matthew 11:14, and that 'Elijah has already come' and was treated as they wished, Matthew 17:12 to 13. The pairing of a prophet with a vengeful queen, Jezebel in 1 Kings 19:2 and Herodias here, is hard to miss.

The line of martyred prophets runs through the rest of the New Testament. Jesus indicts those who 'murdered the prophets,' Matthew 23:29 to 37, and Hebrews 11:36 to 38 speaks of those who 'endured mocking and flogging' and of whom the world was not worthy. Herod's later meeting with Jesus in Luke 23:8 to 11 closes the story: the man who had killed the forerunner now has the Lord Himself standing before him in silence.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wants his readers to see that rejection is not a surprise or a failure but the shape that the kingdom's advance takes. Having shown in chapter 13 how the word is received and refused, he now gives two concrete cases. The home town is the case of the person who cannot get past what he already thinks he knows. Herod is the case of the person who knows more than he will admit and acts against it. Between them they cover the two great obstacles to faith in the Gospel: familiarity and a guilty conscience.

The tone in both scenes is sober. Matthew does not explain away the unbelief of Nazareth or soften the verdict of verse 58. He gives the facts and lets them stand. In the same way he tells John's death without comment, and he does not describe a miraculous rescue. Part of the aim is pastoral. Matthew's readers were facing hostility from their own families and from rulers, and they needed to know that Jesus and His forerunner had been through the same, and that God's purposes were not defeated by it.

The two scenes also prepare for what comes next. Jesus withdraws when He hears of John's death, 14:13, and the cost of being the Messiah becomes plainer. John is the forerunner in his death as in his preaching: the ruler who kills him is a preview of the ruler who will hand Jesus over, and the ending of the Gospel is already in view.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These scenes record what happened, and nothing in them is commanded. The people of Nazareth are not held up as an example; their offence is a warning. The treatment of John is not an endorsement of the violence or of Herod's choices. What is meant to be carried forward is an understanding of how these two forces still work. Familiarity with Christian things, the home church, the family faith, a childhood of Bible stories, can breed a kind of immunity that no longer expects God to speak. A guilty conscience can lead a person to hear of Jesus and think of anything but repentance.

The text also describes a limit on Jesus' public work, 'He did not do many miracles there,' and this should be read as description. It does not say that miracles depend on the sufficient faith of the one asking; many of Jesus' miracles were done for people with little faith or none, and Mark 6:5 notes that He healed a few sick people even there. It is a statement about that place and its settled unbelief, not a rule for the church's healing ministry.

The death of John should not be turned into a formula for suffering. Faithfulness does not guarantee survival, and John's imprisonment led to doubts, Matthew 11:2 to 6, which Jesus treated with patience. The passage invites us to speak truth to power with courage, as John did, while expecting nothing in return but the Lord's approval.

debates.question: Why could Jesus not do many miracles in Nazareth because of their unbelief?

views.label: Not a limit on His power but on His purpose
views.case: Jesus' miracles answered faith and served His mission; He would not perform them as spectacle for hardened hearts, so their unbelief did not weaken His power but removed the fitting occasion for it.

views.label: A real moral connection between faith and blessing
views.case: Scripture repeatedly ties the receiving of God's works to faith; the unbelief of Nazareth genuinely closed them off from the blessings faith would have received, though Jesus' ability was never in question.

debates.bearing: Both affirm Jesus' unlimited power and warn that unbelief shuts people off from the blessings He gives, so that familiarity and offense can rob us of Christ's work among us.

debates.question: What does Herod's execution of John reveal?

views.label: The cowardice of pleasing people over doing right
views.case: Herod knew John was righteous and feared him, yet killed him to keep a rash oath and save face before his guests, a portrait of moral weakness that sacrifices truth to human approval.

views.label: A foreshadowing of Jesus' own fate
views.case: A faithful witness condemned by a reluctant ruler to satisfy others prefigures Pilate handing Jesus over to please the crowd; John's death casts the shadow of the cross ahead.

debates.bearing: Both show the deadly cost of valuing human approval over righteousness and set John's faithful martyrdom as a signpost pointing to the greater rejection of Christ.

debates.question: Who were Jesus' brothers and sisters, verses 55 and 56?

views.label: Children of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus
views.case: The natural reading of the Greek word for brothers, together with the phrase in Matthew 1:25 that Joseph 'did not know her until she gave birth,' suggests younger siblings. This was the view of the early church writer Helvidius, and it is the common Protestant reading.

views.label: Children of Joseph by an earlier marriage
views.case: Some of the church fathers, in the East especially, held that Joseph was a widower with children, so that Jesus' brothers were His step-brothers. This preserves the belief in Mary's perpetual virginity while taking the word 'brothers' at face value.

views.label: Cousins or other relatives
views.case: Jerome argued that the word could cover cousins, since the Hebrew and Aramaic words for brother were used broadly. This became the standard Western Catholic view.

debates.bearing: The text itself does not settle the question, and the first two views are the more natural readings of the Gospel narratives. What matters for the passage is that these were people who knew Jesus from childhood, who at first did not believe, John 7:5, and who later became believers and leaders.

study.originalLanguages:
The people of Nazareth 'took offense' at Jesus, verse 57, using the verb skandalizo, a word built on skandalon, the trigger of a trap or a stumbling block. It is the same word Jesus used in the sower, Matthew 13:21, for the shallow hearer who 'falls away' when trouble comes. In 11:6 Jesus says, 'Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.' The offence is not a mere dislike but a stumbling over the person Himself. They have no problem with His wisdom or His works; what trips them is who He is.

The 'astonished' of verse 54 is ekplesso, to be struck out of oneself, and the same verb is used of the crowds after the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 7:28. Astonishment is not faith. It is possible to be amazed, as the Nazarenes were, and still reject.

The phrase 'miraculous powers,' dynameis, appears both here and in Herod's mouth in 14:2. It is plural, 'powers,' and refers to acts of power as opposed to the 'signs' that others demanded. Herod says that 'miraculous powers are at work in him,' using the verb energeo, from which comes our word energy, which is also used for forces at work in a person. It is an irony of the two scenes that the people who know Jesus best cannot explain where He gets His powers, and the man who had silenced John can only suppose they are John's.

Matthew says Jesus 'was without honor,' atimos, in his hometown. The word is the negative of timē, honour or value. In a culture that ran on honour and shame, to be without it in your own household was a particular wound. The 'prophet' in the saying is generic, but Jesus has applied the title to Himself.

Verse 58 has a careful wording. Mark 6:5 says Jesus 'could not' do any miracle there, and Matthew says He 'did not do many.' The difference is not a contradiction: Matthew's phrasing makes clear that Jesus' power was not limited, while Mark's states the practical effect. Both agree that the cause was unbelief, apistia, a lack of faith.

In 14:5 Herod 'wanted to kill' John and 'feared the people.' In verse 9 the king 'was grieved,' a strong word for distress, but he commanded it, 'because of his oaths and his guests.' The plural 'oaths' is notable. He had sworn to give her whatever she asked, and the reader senses that the commitments of a weak man pile up. Finally, John's disciples 'came and took his body and buried it,' and then 'informed Jesus.' The verb for informing is apangello, the ordinary word for bringing a report, and it shows where John's disciples turned in their grief.

typology.fulfillment: Jesus stands in the line of those whom their own people refused. Jeremiah was threatened by the men of Anathoth, Jeremiah 11:21, and told that his brothers had betrayed him, Jeremiah 12:6; Moses was resisted by those he led; and the psalmist became 'a stranger to my brothers,' Psalm 69:8. The Servant is 'despised and rejected,' Isaiah 53:3. In Jesus the pattern reaches its height: He is not only a prophet who is refused but the one of whom all the prophets spoke, and the refusal at Nazareth foreshadows the larger refusal at Jerusalem. The type is incomplete in that no prophet's rejection saved anyone, but His does.

John dressed as Elijah did, 2 Kings 1:8 and Matthew 3:4, and Malachi 4:5 promised the return of Elijah. Jesus says that John is the Elijah who was to come, Matthew 11:14. The correspondence extends to the opposition: Elijah faced a murderous queen, 1 Kings 19:2, and John faces Herodias. The resemblance has an important difference, since Elijah was spared death and taken up to heaven, while John is killed. Jesus explains in Matthew 17:12 that the Son of Man will suffer in the same way. John's fate is not a defeat of the type but its fulfilment: the forerunner goes before Jesus in suffering.

typology.type: The prophet slain at a king's table, Matthew 14:6 to 11
typology.fulfillment: In Esther's story a king promises 'up to half the kingdom,' Esther 5:3, and that oath is used for life. Herod's offer echoes the formula, but he turns it to death. Another correspondence is Jephthah, whose rash vow drew his daughter into death, Judges 11:30 to 35, and who 'cannot take it back.' Herod is trapped by an oath in the same way, but his is a worse case, because he has the power to refuse and does not. The pattern finds its answer in Pilate, who yields to a crowd and hands over an innocent man, Matthew 27:24 to 26. In both, a ruler prefers his standing to justice.

typology.type: The silent Lord before a mocking king, Matthew 14:1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: Herod wonders about Jesus and says that He must be John risen. Luke 23:8 to 11 completes the story: Herod, who 'had wanted to see Him for a long time,' questions Him and receives no answer, and then mocks Him. The man who silenced the voice of the Baptist now faces the Word and hears nothing. This is not strictly a type but a pattern of judgment, in which a person who has silenced the truth once finds it will not speak again. The pattern is a warning, not a prediction, and it falls short because the story does not tell us Herod's final end.

study.christ:
Jesus appears here as the prophet who is not honoured, and as the one whose rejection was foretold. The proverb is one He applies to Himself, but the whole story of Israel stands behind it. He is the Servant 'despised and rejected by men,' Isaiah 53:3, and the Gospel of John says of Him that He 'came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. The rejection at Nazareth is a small version of a larger one. In Luke's account the people try to throw Him over the cliff, and He walks through the crowd, Luke 4:29 to 30, a picture of a violence that is for the moment restrained and will in due time be allowed.

He is also the one whose forerunner's death points to His own. Jesus says in Matthew 17:12 that Elijah has come and been mistreated, and 'in the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.' The comparison is explicit. Herod's desire to kill John and fear of the people parallels the leaders' plan to kill Jesus and their fear of the crowd, Matthew 21:46. And the weak ruler who gives up a righteous man to save face is a picture of Pilate, who washes his hands in Matthew 27:24. John's death is the first stage of the road that Jesus Himself will walk, which is why it is told in a Gospel about Him.

The passage shows something of His humanity as well. He is known as 'the carpenter's son,' and Mark calls Him 'the carpenter,' Mark 6:3. The incarnation was not a performance; the Son of God took on a trade, a family, a home town. The people of Nazareth take this ordinariness as a reason to reject Him. In fact it is the glory of the incarnation, that He is truly one of us, and Hebrews 2:11 says that He is not ashamed to call us brothers. The very thing the Nazarenes could not see past is the thing that makes Him able to help.

The grief that follows is His own. When Jesus hears of John's death, in the next verses He withdraws to a solitary place, 14:13. The Lord who was faithful to His forerunner and who raised others is not a stranger to sorrow.

There is a caution here too. John's death is not a scene in which each detail represents Jesus, and Herod's banquet is not a coded account of the Lord's Supper. The links above are those that Jesus Himself draws, in Matthew 17:12, and that the Gospels draw by their arrangement of the story. The point that the passage makes about Christ is that He walked the way of rejection from the beginning, and that this was no accident but the Father's plan.
study.god:
This passage raises the hardest question about God in the Gospels: why does He allow His faithful servants to be killed by wicked rulers? Matthew gives no explanation and makes no attempt to soften it. The silence is itself instructive. John, the greatest of the prophets by Jesus' own verdict, Matthew 11:11, dies in prison at the whim of a petty tyrant, and no angel intervenes. The God of this passage is not one whose purposes are measured by the success of His servants. His faithfulness is not the same thing as their safety.

Yet the story also shows that God is not defeated. Herod's conscience is a witness to the fact that a murdered prophet is not silenced. Even from the grave, John's testimony troubles the king. Jesus continues His work, and Matthew's next scene is the great feeding of the crowds. The word of God cannot be bound, as Paul says from his own chains, 2 Timothy 2:9. The judgment on those who kill the prophets is spoken in Matthew 23:34 to 37, and it will come.

God is also patient with unbelief, but not indifferent to it. At Nazareth the offence closes the door to blessing, and Jesus Himself marvels at it, Mark 6:6. This is not the picture of a God who is manipulated by human attitudes, since Jesus' power was never in doubt, but of one who has chosen to give His gifts to those who receive them in faith. Hebrews 11:6 says that without faith it is impossible to please Him, and the refusal of Nazareth is an example. At the same time He does not stop, and 'He went around from village to village, teaching the people,' Mark 6:6. His goodness does not depend on a welcome.

God is just. John told Herod that the marriage was unlawful, Matthew 14:4, and the standard of the Law applies to kings as well as to ordinary people. No ruler stands above God's word. The text assumes that a righteous God has given a law that binds even those who have power to ignore it, and that those who ignore it will answer.

For worship, the passage asks that we honour the Lord in the ordinary and the familiar. It calls us to ask whether we have grown used to Christ, whether our familiarity has left us unable to be astonished, and whether any guilt we carry has been taken to Him or left to fester. It also invites a steady trust in a God whose purposes run through the deaths of His servants and who will vindicate them in His time.

crossReferences.note: Luke's account of the same visit adds that all spoke well of Him at first, that Jesus cited Elijah and Elisha as prophets sent to outsiders, and that the people tried to throw Him from the hill. It shows how quickly admiration became rage and fills in the offence that Matthew only names.

Mark's parallel says that Jesus 'could not' do miracles there except to heal a few sick, and that He was amazed at their unbelief. It clarifies Matthew's brief report and shows that the limit was the effect of unbelief and not a lack of power, since some were still healed.

The LORD tells Jeremiah that even his brothers and his father's household had betrayed him. The prophet's experience of rejection by his own family is the pattern that Jesus names in His proverb, and John 7:5 shows it fulfilled when His own brothers did not believe.

Luke says that John rebuked Herod the tetrarch about Herodias and all the evils he had done, and that Herod added to them by locking John up. It confirms the cause of the imprisonment and shows that John's rebuke covered more than the one marriage.

The Law forbade a man to have relations with his brother's wife. This is the standard behind John's statement that it was not lawful, and it shows that his rebuke was no personal quarrel but an appeal to the Torah that bound kings as well as commoners.

Jezebel vows to take Elijah's life by the next day. Her pursuit of a prophet who had spoken against the royal house parallels Herodias, who held a grudge against John and wanted him dead. John is the Elijah who was to come, and the opposition he meets is the same.

The king offers Esther up to half the kingdom, a formula of royal generosity. Mark 6:23 reports Herod using the same words to Herodias's daughter, which heightens the contrast between a king who promises everything and then is cornered into an act of murder.

John, now in prison, sends his disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who was to come. Jesus answers with the works He is doing and a blessing for those who do not fall away. It shows how John's imprisonment tested him and how Jesus treated his doubt with tenderness.

Jesus tells the disciples that Elijah has already come, was not recognised, and was treated as they pleased, and that the Son of Man will suffer in the same way. The disciples understand that He means John. The death of John is thus explicitly tied to the coming death of Jesus.

Herod finally meets Jesus, and had hoped to see a miracle. Jesus gives no answer to his long questioning, and Herod and his soldiers mock Him. The man who feared that John had risen faces the one who truly will, and treats Him as a joke.

Pilate sees that he is accomplishing nothing, washes his hands and hands Jesus over to be crucified. The ruler who knows a man is innocent and yields to the crowd to preserve his position is the same figure as Herod, and John's death is a rehearsal for the cross.

study.oneStory:
The Bible is, among other things, the story of a people who keep refusing the messengers God sends to them. From Moses at the Red Sea to Jeremiah in the pit, from Elijah under the broom tree to Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned in the temple court, the prophets are heard, opposed and killed. Jesus sums it up in His lament over Jerusalem, 'who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her,' Matthew 23:37. This passage is where that story reaches the two figures at its climax: John, the last of the prophets, and Jesus, the one to whom they all pointed.

It also answers the question that the Old Testament leaves hanging: if the Messiah comes, will Israel receive Him? The answer, at Nazareth, is that many will not, and that the refusal will be not of strangers but of those closest to Him. That prepares the ground for the surprising shape of salvation in the rest of the Gospel. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and the kingdom passes to those who bear its fruit, Matthew 21:42 to 43. Even the offence of Nazareth serves the plan of God, who uses the nation's rejection to bring in the nations, Romans 11:11.

John's death also looks forward. The forerunner prepares the way, and the way is a road of suffering. The ruler who kills him is a sign of the powers that will gather against Jesus, and of the way in which the world treats those who tell it the truth. The martyrs of Revelation 6:9 to 11 are the descendants of John, crying out to God for justice, and told to wait a little longer.

The story ends with vindication. The prophets who were refused will be raised, and the kings who killed them will give an account. In the new creation the 'prophet without honor' will be the King, and the household that refused Him will have been replaced by a family of faith, Hebrews 2:11. John's head on a platter is answered by the Lamb who was slain and who now stands in the midst of the throne, Revelation 5:6, and by the promise to those who are faithful unto death that they will be given the crown of life, Revelation 2:10.

quiz.q: Why did the people of Nazareth take offense at Jesus?

options.text: They could not see past His familiar family and ordinary origins to believe in Him.
options.note: Verses 55-57 show them stumbling over the carpenter's son they thought they knew.

options.text: They rejected His teaching as unwise and dull.
options.note: They were astonished at His wisdom; their offense was over His familiar background, not poor teaching.

options.text: He refused to teach in their synagogue.
options.note: He did teach in their synagogue; the offense was their unbelief, not His refusal.

options.text: He performed no wonders anywhere at all.
options.note: He did mighty works elsewhere; in Nazareth He did few because of their unbelief.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus do few miracles in His hometown?

options.text: Because of their unbelief, not because His power had failed.
options.note: Verse 58 names their unbelief as the reason.

options.text: Because He was too tired from teaching.
options.note: The text names unbelief, not weariness, as the reason.

options.text: Because God forbade Him to help His own town.
options.note: No such prohibition; their unbelief closed them off from His works.

options.text: Because He had lost His ability to heal.
options.note: His power was undiminished; the barrier was their unbelief, not any loss of power.

quiz.q: Why had Herod imprisoned John the Baptist?

options.text: Because John rebuked him for unlawfully marrying Herodias, his brother's wife.
options.note: Verses 3-4 give John's rebuke of the unlawful marriage as the cause.

options.text: Because John had led a revolt against Herod's rule.
options.note: John led no revolt; he rebuked Herod's marriage, a moral, not political, offense.

options.text: Because John claimed to be the Messiah.
options.note: John pointed away from himself to Christ; his imprisonment was over rebuking Herod's marriage.

options.text: Because John refused to pay taxes.
options.note: The issue was John's rebuke of the unlawful marriage, not taxes.

quiz.q: How did John come to be executed?

options.text: Herod, trapped by a rash oath at his birthday feast, granted Herodias's daughter's request for John's head.
options.note: Verses 6-10 show the oath, the dance, and the fatal request.

options.text: Herod eagerly ordered John killed at the first opportunity.
options.note: Herod was actually grieved and had feared the people; he killed John reluctantly to keep his oath, not eagerly.

options.text: The people demanded John's execution.
options.note: The people regarded John as a prophet; the demand came from Herodias through her daughter.

options.text: John died of illness in prison.
options.note: John was beheaded, not taken by illness.

quiz.q: What larger significance does the death of John carry in Matthew?

options.text: The faithful forerunner killed by a cowardly king foreshadows Jesus' own rejection and death.
options.note: John's martyrdom prefigures the cross, where weak rulers condemn the innocent Christ.

options.text: It shows that John's ministry had been a failure.
options.note: John was faithful to the end; his death was martyrdom, not failure, and points ahead to Christ.

options.text: It proves Herod was a righteous but misunderstood ruler.
options.note: Herod is portrayed as weak and cowardly, sacrificing the innocent to save face.

options.text: It means God had abandoned His prophets.
options.note: God's purposes advance through the faithfulness and even death of His messengers; He had not abandoned them.

questions: The people of Nazareth were too familiar with Jesus to believe in Him. Where might overfamiliarity be dulling your own wonder at who Jesus is?
Their unbelief closed them off from Jesus' works. How might your own doubt or hardness be limiting what you receive from Him?
John spoke the truth to a powerful man even though it cost him his freedom and his life. Where is God calling you to stand for what is right despite the cost?
Herod valued his reputation and his guests' opinion over an innocent life. In what areas are you tempted to do wrong rather than lose face before others?
John died faithful, and his death pointed ahead to Christ. How does the example of faithful suffering strengthen you to follow Jesus even when it is hard?

translationNotes.note: The carpenter's son and the naming of Jesus' brothers and sisters show His genuinely ordinary upbringing, which became the occasion of Nazareth's unbelief.
John condemned Herod's marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, as unlawful under Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21.
Herod's grief yet compliance shows a ruler valuing his oath and his guests' opinion above justice, prefiguring Pilate's later condemnation of Jesus to please the crowd.
